title: Ave Regina Caelorum

segments.voice: Yesterday, Alma Redemptoris Mater: the night song of Advent and Christmas. Your line was star of the sea. What did you steer by when the day got choppy? Day one thousand three hundred thirty-six.

Christmas gets packed away, and the song at the end of night prayer changes. The gate and the star step aside. Then come the ashes, and Lent, and the song that stays through it is something that sounds almost like a herald at a palace door: Ave, Regina caelorum. Hail, queen of heaven. Ave, Domina angelorum. Hail, lady of the angels. It's an odd fit at first. Lent is purple cloth, fasting, the long walk toward the cross. Why greet a queen in a season like that? The answer starts in a throne room, a long way back in the Bible. Today's word is this antiphon of Lent.
screen: `CHRISTMAS PACKED AWAY.` → `HAIL, QUEEN OF HEAVEN.` → `A QUEEN, IN LENT?`

segments.voice: First, the throne room. In the Book of Kings, King Solomon is on his throne when his mother, Bathsheba, comes in to speak to him. He stands up, goes to meet her, bows to her, and has a throne set for her at his right hand. In that scene, the king's mother has a seat of honor beside her son. Catholics call Mary queen for that kind of reason: not because she rules in her own right, but because her son is the king. Second, the greetings. Look at how the antiphon talks. Ave, hail. Salve, hail again. Gaude, rejoice. Vale, farewell. It's built almost entirely of greetings, like someone at a doorway who keeps finding another way to say hello. Third, the root and the gate. The song says: salve, radix, salve, porta. Hail, root; hail, gate; from you a light rose on the world. The root reaches back to Isaiah, in the Douay-Rheims: "there shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse." Jesse was David's father. Christians read the new shoot from that old root as a promise of Christ, born into David's family, and they see Mary as the one through whom he came. The gate is the door the light came through. In Lent, a season of waiting for Easter light, the song keeps pointing at the door. Fourth, the farewell. Near the end comes vale, o valde decora: farewell, you who are so beautiful. Then the last request: pray to Christ for us. It is a goodbye said before sleep, and it hands the singers on to her son. So a queen in Lent isn't so odd. Lent walks toward the cross, and this song keeps a door open to the light on the other side.
screen: `QUEEN BECAUSE HER SON IS KING.` · `A SONG MADE OF GREETINGS.` · `HAIL, ROOT; HAIL, GATE.` · `FAREWELL, AND PRAY TO CHRIST FOR US.` · then, large: `THERE SHALL COME FORTH A ROD OUT OF THE ROOT OF JESSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray it at night. Right now is a rehearsal for tonight. Settle, and breathe. Let today go past once, quickly, like a train you're watching from a platform: the morning, the middle, the evening. Don't stop to judge any car. Then, the way the song does, say goodbye to the day. Tonight, before you sleep, do the same, and if you pray, close it with the antiphon's first words, hail, queen of heaven, hail, lady of the angels, and its last request, pray to Christ for us. If you don't, end with one plain farewell to the day, and let it go. The bell holds the time.
Ave Regina Caelorum. Hail, queen of the heavens: the night song of Lent, full of greetings, a root and a gate, and a goodbye before sleep. Today's word.
Your line: hail, queen of heaven. Today, greet someone properly, by name, as if they mattered, and tonight, say a real goodbye to the day. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics who pray the Liturgy of the Hours traditionally close Night Prayer in Lent with the Ave Regina Caelorum, said or sung in Latin chant or in English.

original.note: Latin: hail, queen of the heavens. caelorum is plural.

trapdoor: what you thought: a stately Latin title.
what it means: the night song of Lent: hail, root; hail, gate; farewell, and pray to Christ for us.
what a scholar hears: the queen mother of David's house (3 Kings 2:19), the root of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1), and a Marian antiphon that closes Compline in Lent.

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims (Challoner) wording of Isaiah 11:1 (quoted in part; DR begins 'And there shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up out of his root.').
3 Kings 2:19 (Bathsheba and Solomon) paraphrased. The queen-mother reading is offered as 'that kind of reason', the script's framing of a common Catholic explanation; confirm.
Season: traditionally from the Presentation (February 2) until Holy Week. The script says it begins after Christmas is put away and runs through Lent, per the index. Confirm.
Latin phrases given unquoted with the script's own English; confirm (ex qua mundo lux est orta rendered 'from you a light rose on the world').
Isaiah 11:1 Christian reading (rod = Christ, root through Jesse's line to Mary) attributed to Christians; confirm phrasing.

Editor pass: hook reordered so the song changes when Christmas is put away and stays through Lent (it traditionally begins at the Presentation, before Ash Wednesday), and the northern-hemisphere 'days start to stretch' line cut; the Isaiah reading reworded, since some Fathers read the rod itself as Mary, so the script no longer fixes rod = Christ, root = line ending in Mary.
